title: Arcadia Tenebra - the embodiment of a flawed gem (review)
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n93OGgP941o

Two years after the prototype, Daniel (@dungeondive) reviews the finished Arcadia Tenebra and frames it as the embodiment of two ideas the hobby talks about constantly: the flawed gem and the passion project. The indie roots show everywhere — the thinnest cards he's seen, stapled zine rulebooks, a hand-packed box that arrived crushed in bubble wrap with a thank-you note inside.

He is emphatic that this is a solo game and that it plays best true solo, one character, and warns clearly that it's a mature title: gruesome violence, drugs, crude language, and an encounter involving sexual assault that arrived unannounced.

The review's best passage is a story rather than a mechanism. He drew a lucky card that had him steal Seven League Boots from a gypsy boy at a camp that happened to sit on his actual map position; moving there next turn, he failed a test and drew an unlucky armour lined with needles — the gypsies' revenge — removable only by returning and settling the debt. Randomness, location and narrative aligned by accident, which is exactly the gem inside the flaw.

He also takes the rulebook's advice to roleplay unclear situations seriously, deliberately choosing worse-odds encounters to honour the story, and finds the game much better for it.

----

When a game says "if the rules are unclear, roleplay it" — is that a design gap or an invitation?
